messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sekou had been a school principal for thirty-four years, and for most of that time, he had believed that a school was a sanctuary. He knew every hallway, every classroom, every fire exit in the building, but he had never once thought about them as a way out for himself. That changed on a cool October evening two years ago, when he stayed late to finalize a district budget report. The security guard had already locked the main doors, and Sekou, lost in thought, had not heard anyone else in the building until a man stepped out from the stairwell near the gymnasium.

The man smelled of alcohol, a sharp, sour scent that hit Sekou before the man even spoke. He demanded the keys to the school safe, then the code to the office. Sekou tried to reason with him, to stay calm, but the man became more agitated, shoving him against a locker and pressing something hard into his ribs. For the next forty-five minutes, Sekou was forced to do exactly what he was told: open doors, disarm the alarm, empty the petty cash drawer into a bag. He was not physically injured, but he had never felt so completely stripped of his own will. The man stood too close, his breath thick with alcohol, and Sekou could do nothing but comply. When it was over, the man fled through a side door, and Sekou stood alone in the darkened hallway, shaking, the smell of liquor still clinging to his clothes.

In the weeks that followed, Sekou tried to return to his normal routine. He told himself he had handled it well, that nobody had been hurt, that the money was insured. But the memory did not behave like an ordinary memory. Sometimes, when he least expected it, he would hear the man’s voice in his head—not the words, just the ragged sound of it, close to his ear. Other times, when he deliberately tried to recall the event, he felt nothing at all, as though he were watching a stranger in a movie, and that hollow numbness frightened him more than the fear had. What unsettled him most, however, was the grief. When the memory surfaced fully, he was overcome by a crushing sense of loss, though he could not name what he had lost. He had come to believe that the event happened because of the way he acted—because he had not fought back, because he had not seen it coming, because he had been too trusting, too soft, too old. He began to feel that he could not rely on himself anymore, and if he could not rely on himself, how could he rely on anyone else?

His wife, Mariama, noticed the changes first. He stopped going to the mosque on Fridays, claiming he was tired. He stopped walking to the corner store for his morning newspaper. At work, he found himself scanning for exits the moment he entered any room—the faculty meeting room, the cafeteria, even his own office. He would note the nearest door, the window, the hallway, and he could not stop doing it. If a student ran past him in the corridor, he would flinch, his whole body tensing as though he were about to be struck. The sound of a janitor dropping a mop bucket made him gasp aloud once, in front of a group of parents, and he had to excuse himself. He started to avoid the gymnasium wing altogether, delegating those duties to his vice principal. When a colleague offered him a drink at a retirement party, the smell of whiskey sent a jolt through him, and he set the glass down without taking a sip.

The consequences accumulated slowly. His relationships with his staff became more distant; he stopped holding open-door hours, preferring to communicate by email. He began to feel that everyone was watching him, waiting for him to fail. Mariama complained that he was never present, that he seemed to be somewhere else even when he was sitting next to her on the couch. He knew she was right, but he did not know how to come back.

What finally brought Sekou to seek help was a morning in late November. He had walked into the school auditorium for a student assembly, and before he could stop himself, his eyes had locked onto the emergency exit at the back of the stage. He stood there, frozen, calculating the distance, the number of steps, the angle of the door. The principal of the school could not enter his own auditorium without planning an escape route. That was the moment he realized he could not keep living this way. He was terrified that the man would find him again, even though he knew logically the man was in prison. But the fear did not care about logic. What he hoped for, more than anything, was to walk into a room and see only the room. To smell alcohol and think of nothing at all. To trust himself again.
